run.title: Introduction to inclusive business models
run.objective: Separate organisations by primary objective rather than by what they claim to care about.
explainer: The distinction that runs through this whole course is not about sincerity, sector, or messaging. It is about which objective is primary — the one that wins when two goals pull apart.

A for-profit organisation's primary objective is to maximise profitability, which maximises shareholders' wealth. It may address needs of society, and often genuinely does, but that happens alongside the primary objective rather than in place of it. An inclusive business model reverses the order: its primary objective is to address a specific need of the poor.

The reversal does not make money optional. An inclusive business must still be financially sustainable, because an organisation that cannot cover its costs stops existing and therefore stops serving anyone. So it carries two requirements at once — address the need, and survive — with the need ranked first. That ranking is what the rest of the course tests every business against.

worked.setup: A company selling low-cost water filters says it exists to improve rural health.
worked.move: Ask what it would do if the most profitable segment were urban and middle-class.
worked.because: The answer reveals which objective is primary. Stated intent is not the test; what happens when profit and need diverge is the test.

The goal that wins when two goals conflict — the thing an organisation is actually structured for.
Able to cover its own costs, so it can keep operating without running at a loss.

run.title: Bottom of the pyramid markets
run.objective: State Prahalad's thesis precisely, including the design condition it depends on.
explainer: C.K. Prahalad named the bottom of the pyramid — the base of the economic pyramid, meaning poor people considered as a market rather than as recipients of aid. His claim was that a company designing its product and service in the right manner can make a fortune there.

The argument rests on arithmetic that multinationals had been ignoring. Companies competed for the top of the pyramid, a comparatively small group, while the population below it was very large — roughly 4 billion people earning less than $1,500. Enormous volume at low margin can exceed modest volume at high margin, and nobody was serving it.

The condition is the part most often dropped when the thesis is repeated. "Designed in the right manner" is not decoration — existing products at existing prices do not work at this income level, so the design has to change. The single-serve sachet is the standard illustration: a one-rupee shampoo sachet made the product reachable for someone who could never buy a bottle. Note precisely what it fixes. It does not make shampoo cheaper per wash; it makes the purchase fit a daily cash flow rather than requiring a lump sum.

worked.setup: A consumer goods firm wants to enter low-income markets by discounting its existing large pack by 20%.
worked.move: Redesign the unit of purchase rather than the price of the existing unit.
worked.because: The constraint is often lump-sum cash availability, not the per-unit price. A cheaper large pack still demands money the buyer does not hold at once; a sachet meets the cash flow they actually have.

glossary.plain: The base of the economic pyramid — poor people regarded as a market.
Competition and profit-seeking, here proposed as tools for reaching the poor.
A large company operating across countries, historically competing only for the top of the pyramid.
A single-serve pack that fits a daily cash flow instead of demanding a lump sum.

run.stem: Build the reasoning chain. All three steps must agree before the conclusion is secure.

steps.label: Step 1 · Diagnose the first decision
options: Inclusive business: Reject it as inclusive, because charging any fee to an underserved customer cancels the social purpose the model was built to serve.
